On the right, layout_kamada_kawai() sets the distance between every two nodes to match their number of hops, which straightens the grid into three rows of three." width="100%"} The Kamada-Kawai layout treats every pair of nodes as joined by a spring whose rest length is their shortest-path distance `d_ij`, and minimizes the total spring energy `sum (|x_i - x_j| - d_ij)^2 / d_ij^2`. The `1 / d_ij^2` factor makes nearby pairs matter most, so local structure is drawn faithfully while far-apart pairs are allowed to bend. The result is centered and scaled so the largest coordinate is `scale=`. Compared with `layout_spring()` the layout is deterministic (it starts from a circle, not random positions), edge lengths come out more uniform, and the global shape of paths, grids and trees is usually clearer. Each sweep costs `O(n^2)`, plus an all-pairs shortest-path computation up front, so it is best for graphs of up to a few thousand nodes. NetworkX's `kamada_kawai_layout()` minimizes the same energy with the L-BFGS quasi-Newton method. This method first runs stress majorization sweeps (Gansner, Koren & North, 2004), which move one node at a time to its best position and settle the overall shape reliably, then finishes with L-BFGS, which is much faster through the long, flat stretches of the energy (a path straightening out) where sweeps crawl. The two reach the same kind of layout, though not always the same local minimum. Distances ignore edge direction. Pairs in different components, which have no path, are given a distance one more than the largest finite one (NetworkX uses a fixed `1e6`), so components sit near one another rather than drifting apart. Positions are stored as `[x, y]` lists in the `attr_name=` node attribute; see `layout_circular()`. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [weighted]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Optional[bool]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : If `True`, edge weights (`1` where missing) are edge lengths for the shortest paths, and parallel edges use their lightest weight. If `False`, every edge has length `1`. If `None` (default), follows whether the graph was created as weighted. [initial]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Optional[Union[str, dict]]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Starting positions, as the name of a node attribute holding `(x, y)` pairs or a dict mapping node IDs or labels to pairs; nodes without one start on the circle. If `None` (default), all nodes start evenly spaced on the unit circle, in ID order. [max_iter]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[500]{.dv}]{.doc-parameter-default} : Maximum number of majorization sweeps, and separately of L-BFGS iterations. Default is `500`. [tol]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [float]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[1e-06]{.fl}]{.doc-parameter-default} : Stop once an L-BFGS iteration lowers the energy by at most this fraction. Default is `1e-6`. [scale]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Optional[float]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[1.0]{.fl}]{.doc-parameter-default} : Largest coordinate after rescaling. `None` keeps the raw coordinates, in units of edge length (`center=` is then ignored). Default is `1.0`. [center]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [tuple[float, float]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [(0.0, 0.0)]{.doc-parameter-default} : Center of the layout, as `(x, y)`. Default is the origin. [attr_name]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Optional[str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Node attribute to store the positions in. If `None` (default), uses `"pos"`. If `False` (default), stores the positions on the nodes and returns self for chaining. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Union[dict[int, tuple[float, float]], Graph]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If `return_dict=` is `True`: dictionary mapping node IDs to `(x, y)` tuples. If `return_dict=` is `False` (default): returns self for method chaining. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If `weighted=True` and an edge weight is not positive, `tol=` is negative, an initial position is not a pair of finite numbers, or `scale=` or `center=` is invalid. ::: ## See Also {.doc-see-also} [](`~layout_spring`) : Place nodes with a force-directed spring model. [](`~shortest_path_length`) : Count the edges on a shortest path. [](`~rescale_layout`) : Center and scale stored positions. ## Examples {.doc-examples} Kamada-Kawai places the nodes so that their distances in the drawing match their distances in the graph, counted in edges. With `scale=None` the coordinates are in units of edge length, so the two ends of a path of five edges come out five apart: ::: {#67c39a8b .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec pos = ec.Graph().add_path_graph(6).layout_kamada_kawai( scale=None, return_dict=True ) (x1, y1), (x6, y6) = pos[1], pos[6] round(((x6 - x1) ** 2 + (y6 - y1) ** 2) ** 0.5, 3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 5.0 ``` ::: ::: ### A grid, unfolded From random starting positions, a spring layout can fold a grid over itself, as on the left. Kamada-Kawai on the right lays it flat, since only the flat grid puts every pair of nodes at their distance in the graph: ::: {layout-ncol="2"} ::: {#19ed256f .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} grid = ec.Graph().add_grid_graph([8, 8]) grid.layout_spring(seed=1).plot( layout="pos", width=360, height=360, legend=False ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ::: It needs no seed. It does need the distance between every pair of nodes, which makes it slower than the spring layout on large graphs.
